student.title: First Steps
student.openFile1: From the menu 'Open File' events can be opened. There are two ways to open events:
student.openFile2: Open Local Files: Opens a file from your computer. The file must be in .ig format.
student.openFile3: Open Files from the Web: Opens a file from a list of example files that represent different processes.
student.navigateEvents1: After a file is opened, you can navigate through the events in the file. You can use the arrow keys ← → or the buttons from the top bar.
student.navigateEvents2: The current event number and the total number of events in the file are also displayed in the top bar.
student.changeView1: An event can be displayed in different views. The views can be switched using the buttons 3D, rφ or ρz from the top bar. To return to the initial view, the button can be clicked.
student.changeView2: In the 3D view, the event can also be displayed along an axis. For this, the buttons , and can be used. This can be helpful in determining the particle charge and observing the track curvature.
student.detector1: Under the 'Detector' tab in the control bar on the right side, the various detector elements (in abstract form) can be shown or hidden. The detector elements are divided into different groups that can be selected via the dropdown list. For this, the 'show' checkbox under the respective group must be activated.
student.detector2: A 'real' view of the CMS detector parts can also be displayed. For this, the model of the respective part must be imported via the button 'Import 3D Model' and then 'import file(s) from the Web'. However, it should be noted that the 3D models can be huge in some cases and may slow down the event display. By reloading the page, all imported models can be removed.
student.objects1: The particle tracks in a loaded event can be shown or hidden using the checkboxes under the 'Show/Hide' tab in the control bar on the right side. To keep this setting when switching between events, the checkbox 'Keep Settings' can be activated.
student.objects2: Certain information about the events or the particles can be shown or hidden using the checkboxes under the 'Event Info' tab. For example, the pT and charge of electrons and muons can be displayed by activating the 'Track Info' checkboxes when hovering over the track.
student.selection1: Various cuts can be applied to the loaded events to display only objects that meet certain criteria. The cuts can be set under the 'Momentum Cut' tab in the control bar on the right side. These cuts are for display purposes only and do not affect the event selection later.
student.invariantMass1: Tracks of muons and electrons can be selected by clicking on them, and the invariant mass of these particles can be calculated by pressing <kbd>m</kbd> on the keyboard. The invariant mass will be displayed in a pop-up window. The number of selected tracks can be viewed under the 'Event Info' tab.
student.eventSelection1: Test Selection Cuts on a Specific Event
student.eventSelection2: Under the 'Event Selection' tab, the cuts can be applied to the various particle variables. There are 3 different types of cuts possible:
student.eventSelection3: Number of Particles: Selects events with exactly the number of selected particles (muons, electrons, or photons). For example, events with 2 muons can be selected. This cut is only applied if the checkbox is activated.
student.eventSelection4: Charge Cut: Selects events in which the selected particles have a specific sign of the charge sum. For example, events with a neutral charge sum can be selected.
student.eventSelection5: Momentum Cut: Selects events in which the selected particles meet a minimum pT requirement. For example, events with muons with a pT > 20 GeV can be selected.
student.eventSelection6: MET Cut: Selects events with a minimum or maximum MET. For example, events with a MET > 30 GeV can be selected. The maximum MET cut is only applied if the checkbox is activated.

teacher.title: Installation and Setup Guide
teacher.intro: To start using the event display for your masterclasses, follow these steps to install and set up the software. This guide will demonstrate how to get the application running on your local machine. However, it is also possible to host the application on a web server for easier access by students. For the latter, check with your server provider for specific instructions.
teacher.prerequisites2: For running a local server, this guide provides instructions using Python's built-in HTTP server or Node.js-based http-server. If preferred, other tools can be used as well (e.g., XAMPP, WAMP).
teacher.prerequisites3: Download and install either Python or Node.js, if not already installed. Follow the official installation instructions for the installation.
teacher.prerequisites4: For most UNIX based systems (Linux, macOS), Python is usually pre-installed. For Windows, it is possible to install a python version from the Microsoft Store.
teacher.download1: Download a release of the event display from the official repository (link above). The release is a .zip file containing all necessary files and can be hosted out of the box.
teacher.download2: Extract the contents of the .zip file. For most recent operating systems, this can be done by right-clicking the file and selecting 'Extract All...'.

dev.title: Developer Guide
dev.intro: This guide provides instructions for developers who want to edit, expand functionalities or contribute to the event display project. It covers the setup of the development environment, cloning the repository, installing dependencies, and running the application in development mode.
dev.prerequisites2: Make sure you have Node.js and npm installed on your machine. For these follow the instructions on the official website:
dev.clone1: Either download the repository as a ZIP file or clone the repository using Git (recommended). If you decide to go with git and want to contribute to the project, it is highly recommended to fork the repository to your personal Github account and clone the fork.
dev.git: # Clone the repository using git clone.
dev.git1: # (Adjust the url if your using a fork)
dev.install1: # After npm installs all dependencies, you should be ready to code
dev.compile: # Compile the TypeScript code to JavaScript and bundle everything using webpack
dev.compile1: # For debugging purposes, process using the developement mode for typescript and webpack
dev.run: # For testing, start a server and run the website locally
dev.structure1: The main code files are located in the ts/ directory. The webpage can be found in the index.html file. The processed and bundled files will be output to the dist/ directory. In the dist/ directory, you will also find all assets used by the website including stylesheets, images, and locale files for translations.
